title: You Clicked a Phishing Link
scenario: You're going through candidate emails and click a link in what looked like a routine application follow-up — only after clicking does the page look wrong.

decisions.prompt: The page that opened looks off — a fake-looking login box appears. What's your first move?

options.text: Enter your work login to see if it's really asking for that
options.feedback: Typing credentials into an unfamiliar page is exactly how phishing pages steal them — even a quick "test" entry can hand over a working password.

options.text: Close the tab without entering anything and don't touch the device further
options.feedback: Right call. Not entering anything stops the attack from working, and leaving the device as-is preserves what IT needs to see.

options.text: Take a screenshot to show a coworker before doing anything else
options.feedback: Sharing it around delays the one thing that actually matters here — getting it to IT fast, not crowd-sourcing an opinion first.

decisions.prompt: You didn't enter anything, but the device is still connected to the network. What next?

options.text: Disconnect the device from Wi-Fi and the network
options.feedback: Disconnecting first limits how far anything that did run can spread, before IT even gets involved.

options.text: Leave it connected and keep working — nothing was typed in, so it's probably fine
options.feedback: A link can trigger something the moment the page loads, before you type anything. Staying connected gives it time to spread.

decisions.prompt: Now it's time to loop in IT Security. What do you report, and how fast?

options.text: Report it immediately, including the sender, the link, and exactly what you clicked
options.feedback: Fast, detailed reporting is what lets IT Security contain it before it reaches anyone else — and gives them what they need to act.

options.text: Wait to see if anything actually goes wrong before reporting
options.feedback: By the time something visibly goes wrong, the window to contain it quietly may already be gone.

options.text: Change your password yourself first, then report later
options.feedback: Reporting first means IT can tell you whether a password change is even needed — doing it solo can also overwrite evidence they need.

debrief: Whether it's a link, an attachment, or anything you weren't expecting — STOP before you interact further, VERIFY nothing more before disconnecting, and REPORT immediately with the details. Every minute you wait is a minute IT Security doesn't have.

title: You Found an Unknown USB Drive
scenario: You're doing rounds on deck and find a USB drive taped to a workstation with no label and no obvious owner.

decisions.prompt: No one's claiming it and you're curious who it belongs to. What do you do?

options.text: Plug it into a nearby workstation to check what's on it
options.feedback: Unknown drives can run malicious code the instant they're connected — plugging it in to "just look" is exactly how it gets in.

options.text: Leave it unplugged and don't try to identify the owner yourself
options.feedback: Exactly right — not connecting it removes the risk entirely, and it's not your job to figure out whose it is.

options.text: Ask around the crew mess if anyone's missing a USB drive
options.feedback: Reasonable instinct, but it delays getting it to someone who can actually check it safely, and word can reach whoever planted it.

decisions.prompt: You've left it unplugged. What's the right next step before it gets forgotten in a drawer?

options.text: Check with IT whether there's a safe way to inspect unknown media
options.feedback: This is the right instinct — some teams have an isolated way to check media safely, and asking first avoids guessing.

options.text: Hold onto it and mention it whenever IT is next around
options.feedback: "Whenever they're next around" can mean days — a live threat sitting in a drawer is still a threat.

decisions.prompt: Time to hand it over. What's the move?

options.text: Report it and hand it to IT Security or your security team directly
options.feedback: Handing it over and letting IT determine whether it's safe is exactly how this should end — properly contained, properly checked.

options.text: Drop it at the front desk with a note and move on
options.feedback: It might sit there unnoticed for a while — a direct handover to IT/security makes sure someone qualified actually looks at it.

debrief: Unknown media is one of the easiest ways malware gets onto a system — STOP before connecting anything, VERIFY with IT how to handle it safely, and REPORT it directly so it gets properly inspected, not left in a drawer.

title: Your Laptop Was Stolen
scenario: You're back from a site visit and realize your laptop was stolen from the van during a stop.

decisions.prompt: You just realized it's gone. What's your first move?

options.text: Drive back to the last stop to look for it yourself
options.feedback: Every minute spent searching is a minute IT isn't locking down accounts or triggering a remote wipe — speed matters more than the search.

options.text: Report it to IT Security and your manager immediately
options.feedback: Exactly right — fast reporting is what lets IT act while there's still time to lock things down.

decisions.prompt: IT Security is on the call with you now. What do you give them?

options.text: The device ID or asset tag, if you have it
options.feedback: That's what lets IT act on the right device fast, instead of chasing down details first.

options.text: Just a general description — you'll dig up the exact details later
options.feedback: Vague details slow down the one thing that needs to happen fast: locking down the right device.

decisions.prompt: IT asks what else needs attention. What do you check?

options.text: Ask IT whether a remote wipe or lock was triggered, and change your passwords
options.feedback: Confirming the wipe/lock and rotating your passwords closes the two doors an attacker would actually use.

options.text: Assume IT has it handled and move on with your day
options.feedback: IT handling the device doesn't cover accounts you were logged into elsewhere — those still need attention from you.

debrief: A stolen device with company access is a race against the clock — STOP chasing it yourself, REPORT immediately with what you know, and VERIFY the follow-up (remote wipe, password changes) actually happened.

title: You Suspect a Data Breach
scenario: You notice financial records that shouldn't be accessible are suddenly showing up in a shared folder anyone can open.

decisions.prompt: You've just spotted this. What's your first move?

options.text: Message a few colleagues to see if they've noticed it too
options.feedback: Talking it around — even internally — risks the details spreading before IT Security has confirmed what's actually going on.

options.text: Avoid discussing it publicly or on social media, and don't touch the files
options.feedback: Exactly right — containing the conversation and not touching anything preserves both the evidence and the situation.

decisions.prompt: You haven't touched anything. What do you do next?

options.text: Try moving the folder somewhere more restricted yourself
options.feedback: Fixing it yourself can overwrite exactly the evidence IT Security needs to figure out what happened and how.

options.text: Note down what you observed — what, when, and how — without changing anything
options.feedback: This gives IT Security the details they need without disturbing the scene.

decisions.prompt: You have the details noted. What now?

options.text: Escalate to IT Security right away and leave affected systems running
options.feedback: Reporting fast and leaving systems running preserves the evidence trail IT Security needs to investigate properly.

options.text: Shut down the affected systems to be safe, then report
options.feedback: Shutting systems down can wipe exactly the evidence needed — reporting first, systems untouched, is the safer order.

debrief: A suspected breach is a scene, not a mess to clean up — STOP before discussing or fixing anything, VERIFY what you observed without disturbing it, and REPORT right away so the trained response team can take it from there.

title: You Got a Suspicious Phone Call
scenario: Someone calls the vessel line claiming to be from head office IT, asking you to confirm your login details over the phone.

decisions.prompt: The caller is asking you to confirm your login details right now. What do you do?

options.text: Give a partial answer to seem cooperative without giving everything
options.feedback: Even a partial confirmation can be enough — a caller like this only needs one true detail to build the rest.

options.text: Decline to give out any passwords, codes, or personal information
options.feedback: Exactly right — no legitimate IT request needs you to say this out loud on an inbound call.

decisions.prompt: They push back, asking you to "just confirm" if the account details they read out are correct. What now?

options.text: Confirm or deny the details to move the call along faster
options.feedback: Even confirming "no, that's wrong" tells them something real — the safest answer is no answer at all.

options.text: Hang up and call the official number yourself to verify
options.feedback: Exactly right — calling back on a number you already trust removes their control of the conversation entirely.

decisions.prompt: You've hung up and called back on the real number. What's left to do?

options.text: Report the call to IT Security, noting the caller ID and what they asked for
options.feedback: This gives IT Security what they need to warn others and possibly trace the pattern.

options.text: Let it go since nothing was actually given away
options.feedback: Even an unsuccessful attempt is worth flagging — it likely means others are getting the same call.

debrief: Urgency on a call is a tactic, not a real deadline — STOP before giving out anything, VERIFY by calling back on a number you trust, and REPORT the attempt so others can be warned.

title: Your Screen Just Locked
scenario: A message fills your screen demanding payment to unlock your files. A countdown timer is running.

options.text: Try to pay quickly before the timer runs out
options.feedback: Paying doesn't guarantee your files come back, and it funds the next attack. This also skips reporting entirely, which is what IT Security needs most right now.

options.text: Disconnect the device from the network immediately
options.feedback: Right instinct — this can stop it from spreading to other systems before IT gets involved.

options.text: Post about it in the team chat to warn others
options.feedback: Understandable, but this isn't the fastest route to containment, and it can spread panic before IT has confirmed scope.

decisions.prompt: The device is disconnected. What's next?

options.text: Report it to IT Security immediately, describing exactly what's on screen
options.feedback: This is what actually gets a response moving — IT Security needs to know the details fast to contain it fleet-wide if needed.

options.text: Try restarting the device to see if the message clears
options.feedback: Restarting won't undo it and can make recovery harder — IT needs to see the device in its current state first.

decisions.prompt: IT Security is responding. What do you do while you wait?

options.text: Leave the device disconnected and untouched, and follow IT's guidance
options.feedback: Exactly right — leaving it as-is preserves what IT needs to investigate and recover safely.

options.text: Try a few things yourself to see if you can unlock it
options.feedback: Self-fixing a live ransomware lock risks destroying data or evidence IT could otherwise recover.

debrief: Ransomware wants you to panic and pay — STOP by disconnecting immediately, skip trying to VERIFY anything by paying or self-fixing, and REPORT fast so IT Security can contain it before it reaches other systems.
